stem: A study protocol sets the significance level at 0.05. The investigators explain that this is the chance they accept of reporting a group difference when, in the population, no difference exists.
oneliner: significance level 0.05 + chance of reporting a difference that is not real → which quantity?
ask: Which quantity does this 5% represent?

options.E: P value of the observed result

whyNot.B: Power is the chance of detecting a **real** difference; the stem describes no real difference
whyNot.C: Confidence level is **1 − alpha** (95%), the complement, not the error itself
whyNot.D: Beta is the chance of **missing** a real difference; here a difference is wrongly claimed
whyNot.E: The P value is **calculated from the data**; alpha is the cutoff set before the study

answer: Alpha, the type I error probability
why: Alpha is the **threshold set in advance** for calling a result significant. It equals the chance of a **false-positive** conclusion: rejecting a null hypothesis that is true.

idea.rule: Alpha = probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis (type I error, false positive).
also: Beta = probability of missing a real difference (type II, false negative)
P value < alpha means reject the null

stem: A trial of 40 patients finds no significant difference between a new drug and placebo (p = 0.10). Several larger trials later show that the drug clearly works.
oneliner: small trial + p 0.10 called 'no difference' + drug later proven effective → which error?
ask: Which error did the first trial most likely make?

whyNot.A: Type I error is a **false positive**; this trial reported no effect
whyNot.B: Confounding is a **third variable** distorting an association; the stem names none, and the later larger trials point to a **sample too small** to show the effect
whyNot.C: Selection bias needs **unrepresentative group assignment**; none is described
whyNot.E: Lead-time bias concerns **screening and survival from diagnosis**, not a drug trial

answer: Type II error (beta): a real effect was missed
why: The null hypothesis was **not rejected although it was false**. A small sample gives **low power**, so a **false-negative** result is likely.

idea.rule: Failing to reject a false null hypothesis is a type II (beta) error, a false negative.
also: Common cause: sample too small (low power)
A nonsignificant result does not prove no effect

stem: Investigators plan a trial with an 80% chance of detecting a true 0.4-point difference in symptom score between treatments, using p < 0.05 as the cutoff.
oneliner: 80% chance of detecting a true 0.4-point difference → which quantity?
ask: Which statistical quantity is the 80%?

whyNot.A: Alpha is the **false-positive** threshold (0.05 here)
whyNot.C: The P value is **computed after** the data are collected, not planned
whyNot.D: Beta is the chance of **missing** the true difference; here it would be 20%, not 80%
whyNot.E: Confidence level is **1 − alpha** (95%)

why: Power is the **probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when a true difference of the stated size exists**. It equals **1 − beta**, so 80% power means beta = 20%.

idea.rule: Power = 1 − beta = chance of detecting a real effect of a stated size.
also: Falls when alpha is made stricter

stem: A 47-year-old woman has a positive result on a screening test for an uncommon disease. She asks how likely it is that she truly has the disease.
oneliner: 47F + positive screening test + asks chance of true disease → which measure?
ask: Which test measure answers her question?

whyNot.A: Sensitivity starts from **people with disease** and asks who tests positive
whyNot.B: Specificity starts from **people without disease** and asks who tests negative
whyNot.C: NPV applies after a **negative** result
whyNot.D: LR+ is the **ratio** of the chance of a positive result in diseased vs healthy people; it is **not a probability** of disease

why: Her positive result is already known, so the question is **how many positives are true cases**: **TP / (TP + FP)**, which is the PPV.

idea.rule: PPV = TP / (TP + FP): chance of disease given a positive test.

stem: A screening test for a viral infection is moved from a clinic where 5% of attendees are infected to a previously screened group where 0.2% are infected. The same assay and cutoff are used.
oneliner: same assay + prevalence 5% to 0.2% → which value is lower?
ask: Which value is lower in the new group?

whyNot.A: Sensitivity is a **fixed property** of the test; prevalence does not change it
whyNot.B: Specificity is also **fixed** for the same cutoff
whyNot.D: NPV **rises** when disease becomes rarer
whyNot.E: The false-positive rate is **1 − specificity**, fixed for the **same assay and cutoff**

why: With **fewer true cases**, the same false-positive rate produces a **larger share of false positives among positives**, so PPV falls. Sensitivity and specificity do not depend on prevalence.

idea.rule: Lower prevalence lowers PPV and raises NPV; sensitivity and specificity stay fixed.
also: Screening a low-risk group gives many false positives
Sensitivity and specificity are test properties

stem: Investigators enroll 120 patients with pancreatic cancer and 240 controls without it, then ask each participant about past cigarette smoking.
oneliner: 120 cases + 240 controls chosen by disease + recalled smoking → which measure?
ask: Which measure of association can this study report?

whyNot.A: Relative risk needs **incidence in exposed and unexposed**, which this design cannot give
whyNot.C: Incidence needs **followed people at risk**; here disease status was the starting point
whyNot.D: Attributable risk also depends on **incidence** in each group
whyNot.E: Prevalence in the sample is **set by the investigators' choice** of 120 cases and 240 controls

why: Participants were **picked by disease status**, so the ratio of cases to controls is fixed by the investigator. Only the **odds of exposure** in cases vs controls can be compared, giving an **odds ratio**.

idea.rule: Case-control studies give odds ratios, never incidence or relative risk.
also: Cohort studies give relative risk and incidence
OR approximates RR when the disease is rare
Trials give relative risk and absolute risk reduction

stem: A study of 200 adults reports a Pearson correlation coefficient of +0.6 between LDL cholesterol and high-sensitivity CRP.
oneliner: 200 adults + LDL vs hs-CRP r = +0.6 → which statement?
ask: Which statement best describes this result?

options.A: LDL elevation causes the rise in hs-CRP
options.B: Adults with higher LDL tend to have lower hs-CRP
options.C: The two variables have no linear relationship
options.D: 60% of the variation in hs-CRP is explained by LDL
options.E: Adults with higher LDL tend to have higher hs-CRP

whyNot.A: Correlation shows **association, not causation**
whyNot.B: A **negative** r would mean this; the sign here is positive
whyNot.C: **r = 0** means no linear relationship; 0.6 is moderate
whyNot.D: The share explained is **r squared** = 0.36, or 36%

answer: Higher LDL goes with higher hs-CRP
why: The coefficient runs from **−1 to +1**. The **positive sign** means the two variables move in the same direction; the size (0.6) gives moderate strength.

idea.rule: Correlation coefficient r: sign gives direction, magnitude gives strength, r-squared gives variance explained.

stem: Patients with multivessel coronary disease are assigned by a random process to bypass surgery or to one of two types of angioplasty, then followed for 5 years for death and myocardial infarction.
oneliner: random assignment to surgery or angioplasty + followed forward → which design?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: A cohort study **observes** exposures; here the investigators **assign** them
whyNot.B: Case-control starts from **outcome status** and looks back
whyNot.D: Crossover has each patient receive **more than one treatment in sequence**; here each gets one
whyNot.E: Cross-sectional measures exposure and outcome **at one time point**

why: The investigators **assign treatment by chance** and then follow patients **forward** for outcomes. Random assignment is the defining feature of an RCT.

idea.rule: Random assignment of an intervention plus forward follow-up = RCT.
also: Randomization balances known and unknown confounders
Blinding reduces observer and participant bias
Intention-to-treat keeps the groups as randomized
RCT is the best design for testing treatments

stem: Adults with thyroid cancer and age-matched adults without it are each asked about radiation exposure in childhood.
oneliner: thyroid cancer group + matched healthy group + past radiation recalled → which design?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.B: A prospective cohort starts with **exposure groups** and follows them forward
whyNot.C: A retrospective cohort also starts from **exposure** recorded in the past
whyNot.D: Cross-sectional takes a **single-time snapshot** of a population, not selected cases and controls
whyNot.E: A case series has **no comparison group**

why: Groups were chosen by **disease status** (cancer vs none), and **past exposure** was looked up in each. That is the structure of a case-control study.

idea.rule: Case-control: select by outcome, compare past exposure.

stem: Day-care workers and office workers, none of whom has CMV infection at enrollment, are followed for 5 years, and new CMV infections are counted in each group.
oneliner: day-care vs office workers + infection-free at start + followed 5 years → which design?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: Case-control **begins with people who already have** the disease
whyNot.B: A case series describes patients **who already have** the outcome, with no comparison
whyNot.C: A cross-sectional survey measures everything **at one time**
whyNot.E: An RCT would need the investigators to **assign** the exposure; here jobs were not assigned

why: Groups were defined by **exposure** (job type), were **disease-free** at the start, and were **followed forward** for new cases. That allows incidence and relative risk.

idea.rule: Cohort: select by exposure, follow forward for outcomes.
also: Good for common outcomes and rare exposures

stem: A journal report describes 6 patients who developed the same rare liver injury after starting a newly marketed drug. No patients without liver injury are described.
oneliner: 6 patients with same rare liver injury after new drug + no comparison group → which design?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: Case-control requires a **control group without the disease**
whyNot.B: A cohort follows **exposed and unexposed groups** to compare outcomes
whyNot.D: Cross-sectional estimates **prevalence in a defined population**
whyNot.E: Ecological studies use **population-level data**, not individual patients

why: It describes a **small group with a shared outcome** and has **no comparison group**. Such reports are useful for **generating hypotheses** and flagging rare adverse effects.

idea.rule: Case series = descriptive, no control group, hypothesis-generating.
also: Often the first signal of a rare adverse effect
A single patient report is a case report
Near the bottom of the evidence hierarchy

stem: A researcher emails a survey to every address on a hospital staff list and analyzes the answers of whoever replies.
oneliner: survey emailed to staff list + analyzes whoever replies → which sampling method?
ask: Which sampling method was used?

whyNot.B: Simple random sampling gives **every member an equal chance by random draw**; replies here are self-selected
whyNot.C: Stratified sampling **divides into subgroups** and then randomly samples each
whyNot.D: Cluster sampling randomly picks **whole groups**, such as wards
whyNot.E: Systematic sampling takes **every nth person** from a list

why: The sample is whoever is **easy to reach and chooses to reply**, with **no random selection**. It may not represent the target population, so **selection bias** is a risk.

idea.rule: Nonrandom, easy-access samples are convenience samples and risk selection bias.
also: Random assignment is different from random sampling

stem: Twenty adults with hypertension take drug A for 4 weeks, stop for a 2-week washout, then take drug B for 4 weeks. Each person's blood pressure on A is compared with the same person's blood pressure on B.
oneliner: 20 adults take A, washout, then B + within-person comparison → which design?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: In a parallel-group trial each participant gets **only one** treatment
whyNot.B: A factorial trial tests **two interventions at once in combination** across groups
whyNot.C: A cohort study **observes** exposures rather than assigning them
whyNot.E: Case-control selects people by **disease status**

why: Every participant receives **both treatments in sequence** with a **washout** in between, so each person acts as their **own control**. This reduces between-person variability.

idea.rule: Crossover: each subject gets all treatments in sequence and serves as own control.
also: Needs a washout to prevent carryover
Unsuitable for diseases that are cured
Order of treatments is usually randomized

stem: After a screening program for a cancer begins, tumors are diagnosed on average 2 years earlier than before. Survival counted from diagnosis rises by about 2 years, but patients die at the same age as before. Screen-detected tumors have the same growth rate as tumors found by symptoms.
oneliner: screening finds cancer 2 years earlier + survival from diagnosis up 2 years + same age at death + same tumor growth rate → which bias?
ask: Which bias best explains the result?

whyNot.A: Length-time bias needs screening to pick up **slower-growing** tumors; here screen-detected tumors have the **same growth rate**
whyNot.C: Recall bias affects **exposure history reported** by patients
whyNot.D: Selection bias concerns **how participants were chosen**
whyNot.E: Confounding involves a **third variable** linked to exposure and outcome

why: Screening finds disease **earlier**, so the survival clock **starts sooner**, but death occurs at the **same time**. Survival from diagnosis looks longer while **mortality is unchanged**.

idea.rule: Earlier detection without later death lengthens survival from diagnosis only.
also: Screening bias can make a useless test look good
Compare stage-matched patients to reduce it

stem: A receiver operating characteristic curve plots sensitivity on the y-axis against 1 − specificity on the x-axis, with five cutpoints marked along the curve.
oneliner: ROC curve + five cutpoints + sensitivity vs 1 − specificity → which point has highest specificity?
ask: Which cutpoint has the highest specificity?

whyNot.A: That is the **best balance** of sensitivity and specificity, not the highest specificity
whyNot.B: The diagonal marks a test **no better than chance**
whyNot.C: That is the **highest sensitivity** and the **lowest specificity**
whyNot.D: The middle point has **intermediate** specificity

why: The x-axis is **1 − specificity**, so the point with the **smallest x value** has the **highest specificity**. It is also the point with the **lowest sensitivity**.

idea.rule: On an ROC curve, moving right and up raises sensitivity and lowers specificity.
also: Upper-left corner is the ideal test
Area under the curve measures overall accuracy
Lowering the cutoff (high values = disease) raises sensitivity

stem: Two laboratory methods measure the same sample repeatedly. Method 1 has a coefficient of variation of 2.5%, and method 2 has 3.5%.
oneliner: two lab methods + repeated measures of one sample + CV 2.5% vs 3.5% → what does lower CV show?
ask: What does the lower coefficient of variation of method 1 indicate?

whyNot.A: Accuracy is closeness to the **true value**, which needs a reference standard
whyNot.B: Sensitivity is about **detecting disease**, not repeat-measure scatter
whyNot.C: Validity also means agreement with the **truth**
whyNot.E: Systematic bias is **consistent offset from the truth**; CV does not measure it

why: CV = **SD / mean × 100**, a measure of **relative scatter** across repeat measurements. The method with the **lower CV** gives more **reproducible** results, so it is more **precise**.

idea.rule: Precision = reproducibility (low scatter); accuracy = closeness to truth.
also: A test can be precise but inaccurate
Reliability is another word for precision

stem: A 10-year-old girl is brought unconscious to the emergency department after a car crash, with internal bleeding. Her parents cannot be reached. The surgeon takes her to the operating room immediately.
oneliner: 10F + unconscious after crash + parents unreachable + emergency surgery → which ethical principle?
ask: Which ethical principle most directly guides the surgeon's decision?

whyNot.A: Autonomy is the patient's **right to decide**; she cannot, and consent is **implied** in an emergency
whyNot.B: Nonmaleficence means **avoid harm**, not the duty to act for benefit
whyNot.D: Justice concerns **fair distribution** of resources
whyNot.E: Confidentiality is about **protecting information**

why: The surgeon acts to **promote the patient's welfare** by performing **life-saving treatment**. Acting in the patient's best interest is **beneficence**.

idea.rule: Beneficence = act in the patient's best interest.
also: Emergency exception: treat without consent when delay risks life

stem: A survey of 2,000 adults on a single day asks each person about current cigarette use and whether they have asthma now.
oneliner: Survey of 2,000 adults on one day: smoking + current asthma, measured together → ? → ?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: A cohort follows people **forward over time**; here everyone is measured once
whyNot.C: A case-control study **selects people by disease status**; here all 2,000 adults were surveyed
whyNot.D: Ecological uses **group-level data**, but here individuals are measured
whyNot.E: A case series describes **only patients with a disease**; here all 2,000 adults were surveyed

why: Exposure and disease are measured **together at one point in time** in a sample of the population. This is a **cross-sectional study**, which gives **prevalence**.

idea.rule: One time point, exposure and disease together = cross-sectional.

stem: Researchers compare average daily salt intake with stroke death rates across 30 countries using national statistics. No data on individual people are available.
oneliner: Country-level salt intake vs stroke death rates across 30 countries, no individual data → ? → ?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: Cross-sectional studies measure **individuals**, not countries
whyNot.B: A cohort follows **individuals** forward
whyNot.C: A case-control study compares **individual** cases and controls
whyNot.E: A meta-analysis **pools published studies**, not national rates

why: The unit of analysis is the **population (country)**, with **group-level exposure and outcome** and no individual data. This is an **ecological study**.

idea.rule: Group-level exposure and outcome data = ecological.
also: Fat intake vs colon cancer by country
Air pollution vs asthma rates by city

stem: A new drug is given at rising doses to 30 healthy volunteers to study its absorption, half-life and side effects.
oneliner: New drug, 30 healthy volunteers, rising doses, absorption and side effects → ? → ?
ask: Which stage of drug development is this?

whyNot.A: Phase 2 tests **efficacy in patients** with the disease
whyNot.B: Phase 3 is a **large comparison** in patients
whyNot.D: Phase 4 is **after approval**
whyNot.E: Volunteers are **human**, so this is not an animal study

why: A **small number of healthy volunteers** receiving a new drug to assess **safety, toxicity and pharmacokinetics** is a **phase 1 trial**.

idea.rule: Phase 1 = healthy volunteers, safety and pharmacokinetics.
also: Phase 2: efficacy and dosing in patients
Phase 3: large trial vs standard care

stem: After approval by the FDA, a drug's use is monitored in thousands of patients to detect rare or delayed adverse events.
oneliner: Approved drug, thousands monitored for rare or long-term adverse events → ? → ?
ask: Which stage of drug development is this?

whyNot.A: Phase 1 tests **safety in few volunteers** before approval
whyNot.B: Phase 2 tests **efficacy in a limited number** of patients before approval
whyNot.C: Phase 3 is **pre-approval** comparative testing
whyNot.D: Animal work comes **before human studies**

why: Monitoring a drug **after approval** in a **large population** to find **rare or long-term adverse effects** is **phase 4** (postmarketing surveillance).

idea.rule: Phase 4 = after approval, detects rare adverse effects.
also: Phase 3 is too small to detect rare events
Surveillance continues for the life of the drug

stem: Investigators combine the results of 12 randomized trials of aspirin for stroke prevention into a single effect estimate.
oneliner: Results of 12 RCTs of aspirin pooled into one estimate → ? → ?
ask: Which study design is this?

whyNot.A: A systematic review **without pooling** gives no combined estimate
whyNot.C: A cohort enrolls and follows **new participants**
whyNot.D: Ecological studies compare **population rates**
whyNot.E: A multicenter trial **enrolls patients itself**, not published results

why: **Pooling results of several studies** into one estimate to increase **statistical power** is a **meta-analysis**.

idea.rule: Meta-analysis statistically pools published studies.
also: Greater power than any single trial
Limited by quality of included studies

stem: Of 100 patients with confirmed tuberculosis, 90 have a positive result on a new assay.
oneliner: 100 TB patients, 90 positive on new assay → ? → ?
ask: What does the 90% represent?

whyNot.B: Specificity uses people **without** disease
whyNot.C: PPV's denominator is **all who test positive**
whyNot.D: NPV's denominator is **all who test negative**
whyNot.E: Accuracy needs **non-diseased** people too

why: The denominator is **all people with disease** (100), and the numerator is those who test positive (90): **TP / (TP + FN) = 90/100 = 90%**. This is the **sensitivity**.

idea.rule: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN), among the diseased.

stem: Of 200 healthy controls, 190 have a negative result on a new test.
oneliner: 200 healthy controls, 190 test negative → ? → ?
ask: What does the 95% represent?

whyNot.A: Sensitivity uses people **with** disease
whyNot.B: NPV's denominator is **all who test negative**
whyNot.C: PPV's denominator is **all who test positive**
whyNot.D: Prevalence is the proportion **with disease**

why: The denominator is **all people without disease** (200), and the numerator is those who test negative (190): **TN / (TN + FP) = 190/200 = 95%**. This is the **specificity**.

idea.rule: Specificity = TN / (TN + FP), among the non-diseased.

stem: A positive result on a test is reported as being many times more likely in people with the disease than in people without it.
oneliner: Positive result X times more likely in diseased than non-diseased → ? → ?
ask: Which measure is this?

whyNot.A: PPV depends on **prevalence** and is a proportion
whyNot.C: An odds ratio compares **exposure or outcome odds**, not test results
whyNot.D: Relative risk compares **risk between exposure groups**
whyNot.E: Specificity is a **proportion**, not a ratio of rates

why: LR+ = **sensitivity / (1 − specificity)**: how much more likely a positive result is in the **diseased** than the **non-diseased**. It does **not depend on prevalence** and multiplies **pretest odds**.

idea.rule: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity).

stem: In the emergency department, troponin and an ECG are ordered at the same time. The myocardial infarction work-up continues if either result is abnormal.
oneliner: Troponin and ECG done together, positive if either abnormal → which testing strategy?
ask: Which testing strategy is being used?

whyNot.B: Serial testing runs tests **one after another**, not at the same time
whyNot.C: Screening is applied to **asymptomatic people**, and the stem does not describe that
whyNot.D: Confirmatory testing is a **second test after a first positive**, not simultaneous
whyNot.E: Repeat testing means **the same test again**, but two different tests are used here

why: Both tests are done **simultaneously** and **either positive counts**. This parallel strategy **raises sensitivity** (fewer missed infarcts) at the cost of **lower specificity**.

idea.rule: Parallel testing (either positive) raises sensitivity and lowers specificity.
also: Serial testing (all must be positive) raises specificity and lowers sensitivity
Parallel testing suits dangerous diseases where misses are costly
Serial testing suits confirming a diagnosis before risky treatment

stem: A scale is checked with a standard weight of 70.0 kg. Three repeat readings are 72.1, 72.0 and 72.1 kg.
oneliner: Scale reads 72.1, 72.0, 72.1 kg for a 70.0-kg standard → which description fits?
ask: Which description best fits these measurements?

whyNot.A: Readings are **about 2 kg above** the true value, so not accurate
whyNot.B: Readings are **tightly clustered**, so they are not imprecise
whyNot.C: The readings **agree closely with each other**, so precision is present
whyNot.D: The **consistent offset** points to systematic error, not random scatter

why: The readings **cluster tightly** (precise) but sit **2 kg from the true value** (inaccurate). A consistent offset like this is **systematic error**.

idea.rule: Precision is closeness of repeated readings; accuracy is closeness to the true value.
also: Reliability is another word for precision
Validity is another word for accuracy

stem: In a town of 10,000 adults free of diabetes, 50 develop new diabetes over one year.
oneliner: 10,000 disease-free adults, 50 new diabetes cases in one year → which measure?
ask: Which measure is 50 per 10,000 per year?

whyNot.A: Prevalence counts **existing cases** at one time, not new ones
whyNot.C: Attributable risk is a **difference between exposed and unexposed**, and no exposure is given
whyNot.D: Case fatality rate needs **deaths among those with disease**
whyNot.E: Mortality rate counts **deaths**, and none are mentioned

why: **New cases** arising over a **period** among those **at risk** (disease-free) give the **incidence**: 50 / 10,000 = 5 per 1,000 per year.

idea.rule: Incidence = new cases in a period / population at risk.
also: Prevalence = all existing cases / total population at a time
Incidence needs a disease-free starting population

stem: A trial plots a stepwise curve of the proportion of patients alive over 5 years. Some patients were lost to follow-up before the end.
oneliner: Stepwise curve of proportion alive over 5 years, some patients lost to follow-up → which method?
ask: Which analysis method produced this curve?

whyNot.A: Linear regression models a **continuous outcome**, not time to an event with dropouts
whyNot.B: Chi-square compares **categorical proportions at one point**, with no time axis
whyNot.C: An ROC curve plots **sensitivity against 1 − specificity**, not survival
whyNot.E: Pearson correlation measures **linear association of two variables**

why: A **stepwise** curve of **survival over time** that handles **censored** patients is the **Kaplan-Meier (product-limit)** estimate. The curve drops at each death.

idea.rule: Kaplan-Meier estimates survival over time while accounting for censoring.
also: Log-rank test compares two Kaplan-Meier curves
Cox proportional hazards gives a hazard ratio
Censored = event not observed by end of follow-up

stem: A cohort study follows smokers and nonsmokers for 10 years. Lung cancer develops in 20 per 1,000 smokers and 2 per 1,000 nonsmokers. The investigators report a single result of exactly 10.
oneliner: Cohort over 10 years: new lung cancer 20/1,000 smokers vs 2/1,000 nonsmokers, result exactly 10 → which measure?
ask: Which measure of association was reported?

whyNot.B: Odds ratio would be (20/980) / (2/998) ≈ **10.2**, not exactly 10, and it is the usual measure of **case-control** studies
whyNot.C: Attributable risk is the **difference**, 18 per 1,000, not a ratio
whyNot.D: Absolute risk reduction is a **difference** for a **protective treatment**, not a ratio for a harmful exposure
whyNot.E: Prevalence ratio compares **existing cases at one time**, but these are **new cases over 10 years**

why: Cohort studies give incidences, and the **ratio exposed / unexposed** is the **relative risk**: (20/1,000) / (2/1,000) = **10**.

idea.rule: Relative risk = incidence in exposed / incidence in unexposed.
also: Attributable risk = risk exposed − risk unexposed

stem: In a trial, stroke occurs in 10% of patients on placebo and 6% on the study drug. The investigators report the 4% difference.
oneliner: Stroke 10% on placebo vs 6% on drug, 4% difference reported → which measure?
ask: Which measure is the 4% difference?

whyNot.A: Relative risk reduction is the **proportion** 4/10 = 40%
whyNot.C: Relative risk is a **ratio**, 6/10 = 0.6
whyNot.D: Attributable risk percent describes **excess risk from an exposure**, not a treatment benefit
whyNot.E: Odds ratio is a **ratio of odds**, not a difference

why: **Control rate minus treated rate** is the **absolute risk reduction**: 10% − 6% = **4%**. **NNT = 1 / ARR** = 1 / 0.04 = **25**.

idea.rule: ARR = control event rate − treated event rate; NNT = 1/ARR.
also: Relative risk = treated rate / control rate

stem: A drug causes bleeding in 3% of patients, versus 1% on placebo. The authors report a result of 50.
oneliner: Bleeding 3% on drug vs 1% on placebo, authors report 50 → which measure?
ask: Which measure is 50 here?

whyNot.A: NNT counts patients treated to **prevent** one event, not to cause one
whyNot.B: Relative risk would be **3 / 1 = 3**
whyNot.D: Attributable risk percent would be **(3 − 1) / 3 = 67%**
whyNot.E: Odds ratio is about **3.1**, not 50

why: Attributable risk = 3% − 1% = **2%**. **NNH = 1 / attributable risk** = 1 / 0.02 = **50** patients treated per extra bleed.

idea.rule: NNH = 1 / (risk exposed − risk unexposed).
also: NNH uses harm; NNT uses benefit
Both are rounded to whole patients

stem: A case-control study of coffee intake and pancreatic cancer draws its controls from patients on a gastrointestinal inpatient ward.
oneliner: Coffee and pancreatic cancer case-control, controls from GI inpatient ward → which bias?
ask: Which bias is most likely?

whyNot.A: Recall bias concerns **memory of past exposure**, not who is chosen as control
whyNot.B: Confounding needs a **third variable** tied to both coffee and cancer
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias belongs to **screening and survival time**
whyNot.D: Observer bias is **unblinded measurement**, not control selection

why: **Hospital controls** differ from the **source population** (GI inpatients may drink less coffee because of their illness). This is **Berkson bias**, a type of **selection bias**.

idea.rule: Hospital-based controls cause Berkson bias, a form of selection bias.
also: Selection bias: study groups not representative
Healthy worker effect is another selection bias
Loss to follow-up can cause selection bias

stem: Factory workers exposed to a solvent are found to have lower mortality than the general population.
oneliner: Solvent-exposed factory workers have lower mortality than the general population → which bias?
ask: Which bias best explains this result?

whyNot.A: Recall bias requires **self-reported past exposure** and a case-control design
whyNot.C: Lead-time bias applies to **screening detection time**
whyNot.D: Hawthorne effect is **behavior change from being observed**
whyNot.E: Measurement bias is **faulty data collection**, not who is in the group

why: Working people are **healthier than the general population**, which includes the sick and disabled. Comparing the **employed group** with it **hides harm** and is a **selection bias**.

idea.rule: The healthy worker effect makes occupational groups look healthier than the general population.
also: Use an employed comparison group to avoid it
It is a type of selection bias

stem: In a periodic screening program, tumors found by screening are smaller and slower-growing than tumors discovered between screens.
oneliner: Screen-detected tumors smaller and slower-growing than interval tumors → which bias?
ask: Which bias is shown?

whyNot.A: Lead-time bias is **earlier diagnosis lengthening apparent survival**, not tumor behavior
whyNot.B: Recall bias applies to **remembered exposures**
whyNot.C: Observer bias is a **measurer's expectation** shaping results; the stem describes **tumor growth rate**, not rating
whyNot.E: Confounding needs a **third variable** linked to exposure and outcome

why: Screening at intervals catches **slow-growing, less aggressive** disease, which stays detectable longer. Screen-detected cases look as though they do better: **length-time bias**.

idea.rule: Screening favors slow-growing disease, making screen-detected cases look more favorable.
also: Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis, same death time
Interval cancers tend to be aggressive
Mortality rather than survival avoids both biases

stem: Mothers of infants with birth defects report more drug use in pregnancy than mothers of healthy infants, based on a questionnaire.
oneliner: Mothers of infants with birth defects report more drug use than mothers of healthy infants → which bias?
ask: Which bias is most likely?

whyNot.A: Selection bias concerns **how participants were chosen**
whyNot.B: Observer bias is the **researcher's** expectation, not the mothers' reports
whyNot.D: Lead-time bias applies to **screening and survival**
whyNot.E: Confounding needs a **third variable**, and none is given

why: Mothers of affected infants **search their memory harder** for exposures, so exposure is **reported differently** between groups. This **differential misclassification** is **recall bias**, typical of **case-control** studies.

idea.rule: Cases remember or report exposures more completely than controls (recall bias).
also: Records or prospective data reduce it

stem: Coffee drinkers are found to have more lung cancer than non-drinkers. Coffee drinkers also smoke more. After stratifying by smoking, coffee is no longer linked to lung cancer in any stratum.
oneliner: Coffee drinkers get more lung cancer and smoke more; link vanishes in every smoking stratum → what explains the association?
ask: What best explains the association?

whyNot.A: Effect modification means a real effect that **differs across strata**; here the link **vanishes in every stratum**
whyNot.B: Recall bias concerns **memory of exposure**
whyNot.C: Selection bias concerns **how participants were chosen**
whyNot.D: Lead-time bias belongs to **screening**

why: **Smoking** is linked to both **coffee** and **lung cancer**, so it **distorts** the association. Adjusting for it makes the coffee link **disappear**: **confounding**.

idea.rule: A confounder is associated with both exposure and outcome and is not on the causal pathway.
also: Control by matching, stratification or regression
Confounding is removed by adjustment, effect modification is reported

stem: A trial finds a drug lowers stroke risk in men (RR 0.5, 95% CI 0.4 to 0.6) but not in women (RR 1.0, 95% CI 0.9 to 1.1). The difference between the sexes is statistically significant.
oneliner: Drug lowers stroke risk in men (RR 0.5) but not women (RR 1.0), sex difference significant → what does this show?
ask: What does this result show?

whyNot.A: Confounding **distorts** a crude association that **disappears on stratifying**; here the strata give **different real effects**
whyNot.C: Selection bias concerns **who was enrolled**, and nothing about enrollment is described
whyNot.D: Recall bias concerns **memory of exposure**
whyNot.E: The sex difference is **statistically significant** with narrow CIs, so chance is unlikely

why: The **effect differs by stratum** of sex, and the difference is **significant**, so it is a true difference in effect. This is **effect modification**, reported separately rather than adjusted away.

idea.rule: Effect modification means the exposure effect truly differs across levels of a third variable.
also: Confounding is adjusted away; effect modification is not

stem: In a randomized trial of an antidepressant, all patients take identical-looking pills. Neither the patients nor the raters who score depression know the assignment, and the codes are held by the pharmacy.
oneliner: Antidepressant RCT, identical pills, patients and raters unaware of assignment → what is this feature called?
ask: What is this design feature called?

whyNot.A: Single-blind hides assignment from **only one group**; here **patients and raters** are both unaware
whyNot.B: Randomization is **how groups are formed**, not who is masked
whyNot.D: Matching pairs **participants by characteristics**
whyNot.E: Open-label means **everyone knows**

why: **Patients and raters** are both unaware of assignment, thanks to **identical pills**. This **double-blinding** reduces **patient (placebo) bias** and **observer bias**.

idea.rule: Double-blinding hides assignment from both participants and investigators.
also: Randomization reduces selection bias and confounding

stem: An RCT is unblinded and has much more dropout in one arm than the other. Its results may be wrong even for the patients who were enrolled.
oneliner: Unblinded RCT with uneven dropout, results may be wrong even for enrolled patients → which property is threatened?
ask: Which property is threatened?

whyNot.B: External validity concerns **people outside the study**
whyNot.C: Reliability is **repeatability** of measurements
whyNot.D: Power is the ability to **detect a true effect**; the problems described are **bias**, not sample size
whyNot.E: Precision is **spread of repeated values**, not freedom from bias

why: The problem lies **within the study**: **bias** from lack of blinding and uneven dropout. **Internal validity** asks whether results are correct **for the study subjects**.

idea.rule: Internal validity is whether results are true for the study sample, free of bias and confounding.
also: Randomization and blinding support internal validity
Internal validity comes before external validity
Differential loss to follow-up threatens it

stem: A trial enrolled only men aged 20 to 40. A physician wants to apply the results to elderly women.
oneliner: Trial of men aged 20-40, physician applies results to elderly women → which property is limited?
ask: Which property is limited?

whyNot.A: Internal validity concerns **bias within the study**, and none is described
whyNot.B: Reliability is **repeatability**
whyNot.C: Precision is **spread of repeated values**
whyNot.D: Accuracy is **closeness to the true value**, not applicability to other groups

why: The **narrow sample** limits applying the findings to **people outside it**. That is **external validity (generalizability)**.

idea.rule: External validity is whether results apply to people outside the study sample.
also: A study can be internally valid but not generalizable

stem: Clinic staff wash their hands more often after learning that researchers are recording hand hygiene.
oneliner: Staff wash hands more after learning researchers are recording → which effect?
ask: Which effect explains the change?

whyNot.A: Placebo effect needs **an inactive treatment** and expectation of benefit
whyNot.C: Pygmalion effect is **researcher expectation** influencing results
whyNot.D: Recall bias concerns **remembered exposure**
whyNot.E: Lead-time bias belongs to **screening**

why: The staff **know they are observed** and **change their behavior**, with no intervention involved. That is the **Hawthorne effect**.

idea.rule: The Hawthorne effect is behavior change caused by awareness of being observed.
also: Blinding and unobtrusive measurement reduce it
Placebo effect is expectation of benefit from inactive treatment
Pygmalion effect is the investigator's expectation affecting outcome

stem: In a trial for chronic back pain, 35% of patients given sugar pills report less pain. Only 5% of a no-pill group, seen at the same visits, report less pain.
oneliner: Chronic back pain: 35% better on sugar pills vs 5% of a no-pill group seen at the same visits → which effect?
ask: Which effect explains the improvement?

whyNot.A: The no-pill group is **observed at the same visits** yet barely improves, so observation alone does not explain it
whyNot.B: Regression to the mean would affect the **no-pill group equally**, but only 5% of them improve
whyNot.C: Recall bias concerns **remembered exposure**
whyNot.E: Confounding needs a **third variable**

why: An **inactive treatment** led to **subjective improvement** beyond a **no-pill group** seen just as often, because patients **expected benefit**. That is the **placebo effect**.

idea.rule: Placebo effect is improvement from expectation after an inactive treatment.
also: Placebo controls separate drug effect from expectation
Strongest for subjective outcomes such as pain
Blinding keeps the placebo effect equal in both arms

stem: Hospital length-of-stay data show most stays are short, with a few very long stays.
oneliner: Hospital length-of-stay: most short, a few very long → order of mean, median, mode?
ask: How are the central measures ordered?

whyNot.A: Equal measures occur in a **symmetric normal** distribution
whyNot.B: This order fits a **tail to the left**, not long outliers on the right
whyNot.D: The mean sits **toward the tail**, so it exceeds the median here
whyNot.E: The mean is **pulled up** by the long stays, not below the median

why: A few very long stays form a **right tail** (**positive skew**). The **mean is pulled toward the tail**, the **mode** is at the peak, and the **median** is between: **mean > median > mode**.

idea.rule: In positive skew the mean is pulled toward the right tail: mean > median > mode.

stem: A health survey records the yearly incomes of 20 residents of a small town. Nineteen earn between $30,000 and $70,000, and one earns $2 billion. The report must describe a typical resident's income.
oneliner: 20 incomes + one $2 billion outlier → best typical value?
ask: Which summary statistic best describes a typical resident's income?

whyNot.A: The **mean is dragged upward** by the single $2 billion income, above all 19 other residents
whyNot.B: With incomes spread from $30,000 to $70,000, a mode may be **absent or unstable**
whyNot.D: Midrange is (minimum + maximum) / 2, about **$1 billion**, set by the outlier
whyNot.E: **Spread**, not a typical value, and inflated by the outlier

why: The **median is the middle value** once the data are ranked, so one extreme income barely moves it. The mean would be pulled toward the billionaire, which makes it a poor summary of **skewed data**.

idea.rule: Skewed data or outliers: use the median; symmetric data: mean, median and mode agree.
also: Standard deviation and range describe spread, not center

stem: Five studies each report the correlation between daily sodium intake and a different physiologic measure: r = +0.4, r = -0.8, r = +0.1, r = 0 and r = +0.6.
oneliner: Five studies: r = +0.4, -0.8, +0.1, 0, +0.6 → strongest relationship?
ask: Which result shows the strongest relationship?

whyNot.A: Weaker: **|0.4| is smaller than |0.8|**
whyNot.C: Nearly no relationship: **|0.1|**
whyNot.D: **No linear relationship** at all
whyNot.E: Weaker: **|0.6| is smaller than |0.8|**, even though it is positive

why: The **size** of r, ignoring the sign, gives **strength**; the sign gives only **direction**. With |-0.8| the largest, it is the strongest, and its direction is inverse.

idea.rule: Strength = |r|; direction = sign; r ranges from -1 to +1.
also: r squared gives the proportion of variance explained

stem: A 60-year-old man is told the risks, benefits and alternatives of a recommended hernia repair. He understands them, says he does not want the operation, and his surgeon accepts the decision and documents it.
oneliner: 60M + competent + informed refusal of surgery + surgeon accepts → which principle?
ask: Which ethical principle does the surgeon's action best reflect?

whyNot.A: Acting for the patient's benefit; here the surgeon **does not act on the recommendation**
whyNot.B: Avoiding harm; no harm is being weighed in this decision
whyNot.D: **Fair distribution** of care; no allocation issue is described
whyNot.E: **Keeping promises and loyalty** to the patient, not respecting a refusal

why: A competent patient who understands the information has the **right to accept or refuse treatment**. Honoring an **informed refusal** is **autonomy**.

idea.rule: Autonomy = the competent patient decides.
also: Respecting a patient's choice of physician

stem: A 34-year-old woman asks for an antibiotic for 3 days of runny nose and sore throat with a low fever and a negative rapid strep test. Her physician explains this is a viral cold and declines, since the drug would not help and could cause rash, diarrhea or Clostridioides difficile infection.
oneliner: 34F + viral cold + asks for antibiotic + physician declines to avoid harm → which principle?
ask: Which ethical principle does the physician's decision best reflect?

whyNot.B: Acting to **do good**; no benefit exists here, so the point is avoiding harm
whyNot.C: Her wish for the drug is **not what decides** the choice
whyNot.D: **Fair allocation**; not the issue
whyNot.E: **Truth telling**; the physician is honest, but the decision rests on harm

why: The drug offers **no benefit** and carries **risk**, so the physician withholds it. Weighing risk against benefit to **avoid harm** is **nonmaleficence**.

idea.rule: Nonmaleficence = first, do no harm.
also: Stopping a drug with dangerous interactions

stem: A transplant program ranks candidates for a donor liver using only blood type compatibility, severity of liver disease and time on the list. A major financial donor to the hospital and a wealthy executive are both on the list, and neither is moved ahead.
oneliner: Donor liver + ranking by medical criteria only + wealth and fame ignored → which principle?
ask: Which ethical principle does this policy best reflect?

whyNot.A: Concerns an **individual patient's own choice**
whyNot.B: Doing good for one patient; the policy is about **fairness among many**
whyNot.C: Avoiding harm to a patient, not **allocation of a scarce resource**
whyNot.D: **Keeping information private**; no information issue here

why: A **scarce resource** is given by **medical criteria alone**, treating everyone equally regardless of wealth or fame. Fair distribution is **justice**.

idea.rule: Justice = fair allocation and equal treatment.
also: Treating patients the same regardless of insurance

stem: A 45-year-old man smokes a pack a day. He tells his physician, 'I know I should quit, and I may try in the next few months,' but he has set no date and taken no steps.
oneliner: 45M + smoker + knows he should quit + may try in months + no plan → which stage?
ask: Which stage of change is he in?

whyNot.A: Would **deny or not see** a problem
whyNot.B: Has a **plan and date**, usually within a month
whyNot.C: Is **actively changing** behavior
whyNot.E: Has **sustained** the change for 6 months or more

why: He **acknowledges the problem** and plans to change within **6 months**, but has not started. That is **contemplation**.

idea.rule: Contemplation: aware and ambivalent, planning within 6 months.
also: Action: change under way for under 6 months
Maintenance: change held for 6 months or more
